THE RULES OF THE GAME

Don't learn to code.
Learn to make things.

You're the editor and the AI is your coding partner. Your job is to choose an interesting question, test the results against the data, and make something a reader can use.

01 / 5–8 MINPick a missionOr dream up your own.
02 / 8–20 MINBuild the simplest versionOne HTML file, one working feature.
03 / 20–26 MINFact-check the appVerify counts, units, and blanks.
04 / 26–40 MINImprove and demoPolish if it works. Share what you learned.

ONE SHARED SOURCE

Meet your dataset.

Everyone works from the exact same NASA Exoplanet Archive CSV. Download it here, then load it directly into your own webpage using a file picker. No NASA API or internet connection is needed to run the result.

SAME CSV · EVERY TEAM
6,375 unique planets

40,194 source rows · 4,780 host stars · 11 discovery methods · 11 columns

The full ~3.8 MB CSV is included inside this webpage, so the download works offline in modern browsers.

Important: multiple rows describe the same planet. Use default_flag = 1 for a one-record-per-planet view. The 6,375 count refers to this workshop snapshot, not NASA's live total.

THE 11 FIELDS YOUR APP CAN USE
pl_namePlanet name
hostnameHost star
disc_yearDiscovery year
discoverymethodDiscovery method
disc_facilityDiscovery facility
pl_radeRadius · Earth radii
pl_bmasseBest mass estimate · Earth masses
pl_orbperOrbit length · days
pl_eqtModeled equilibrium temperature · K
sy_distDistance · parsecs
default_flagPreferred planet record
THE JOURNALISM CHECKPOINT

Make it work.
Then make it true.

Three tests every team should run before declaring victory — no matter how beautiful the AI-generated page looks.

01 ↗

Count planets, not records.

A correct one-planet-per-row analysis should have 6,375 planets, not 40,194 source rows.

02 ◌

Unknown is not zero.

Missing mass, radius and temperature values must be shown as unknown and excluded from calculations that need them.

03 ✓

Does the science make sense?

Check that your tool uses the right units, doesn’t invent missing information, and doesn’t make claims the data can’t support. For example, a planet’s estimated temperature doesn’t tell us whether it could support life.
